warmup.q: payments has six columns and 1,000,000 rows in a PostgreSQL heap of about 66 MB. amount_cents is a bigint. Roughly how much does SELECT sum(amount_cents) FROM payments read, with no index?
options: About 8 MB: one bigint per row
All of it, about 66 MB: the amounts are spread through every page
About 33 MB: half the pages on average
Almost nothing: PostgreSQL keeps a running sum per column
warmup.why: A heap page holds whole rows, so every page contains some amounts and the scan must read every page: 8,404 pages, 66 MB, in the first Try it. Reading only 8 MB needs the amounts stored together, which is what a column store does. PostgreSQL keeps no running sums; pg_stats has samples and histograms, not totals.

sections.h: A row store reads every column to sum one
sections.html:
Lesson 9 showed that analytics engines process values in batches from one column. This lesson stores them that way. SELECT sum(amount_cents) FROM payments needs 8 bytes from each row. In the Try it, payments has six columns and 1,000,000 rows, and PostgreSQL reads all 8,404 pages of the table, 66 MB, to answer it. The query uses one column and the scan pays for six.

That follows from how lesson 2's heap stores rows. A heap page holds whole rows one after another, each a 24-byte header followed by its six values, 64 bytes per row here. The amounts are spread through every page, so the scan reads every page, and most of each page is ids, merchant ids, currencies, statuses and timestamps. Keeping complete rows together is the row layout, also called the N-ary storage model (NSM).

For the work a payments service does all day, the row layout is right. Inserting a payment writes one row into one page. Fetching payment 42 by its primary key reads one page and gets every column at once. An analytics query is the opposite case: a few columns of millions of rows. The finance team's monthly report sums amounts by currency over 50 million payments and needs two columns out of six.

Version 2 turns the table on its side: keep each column in its own array, the values in row order. Row 1 is the first value of every array, row 2 the second, so the database can put any row back together by its position. sum(amount_cents) now reads one array of 1,000,000 x 8 bytes = 8 MB instead of 66 MB, before any compression. That is the column layout, or decomposition storage model (DSM).

It has a price. Inserting one payment writes to six arrays, and fetching one whole payment reads from six places. Column stores accept that because their users load data in big batches and read it with big scans. They also don't keep a column as one endless file: they cut the table into row groups and store each column of a row group separately. DuckDB's row groups hold 122,880 rows, and a Parquet file is a series of row groups, each with one column chunk per column (the Batch track's lesson on Parquet opens one byte by byte). A scan of one column reads one chunk per row group, and the chunk is the unit that the next two sections compress and skip.

try.title: Count the pages a one-column sum reads
steps: From labs/, start PostgreSQL with docker compose -f env/postgres.yml up -d --wait and open psql with docker compose -f env/postgres.yml exec db psql -U sfz.
Create payments with six columns and 1,000,000 rows (the first statement drops it if an earlier lesson left one). The next Try its use it too.
Read the heap's size, the average row width and the width of the amount. Predict how many pages sum(amount_cents) touches, then check Buffers in the plan.

code.title: psql
code.html: DROP TABLE IF EXISTS payments, shuffled CASCADE; CREATE TABLE payments (id bigint, merchant_id int, currency text, status text, amount_cents bigint, created_at timestamp); INSERT INTO payments SELECT g, 1 + (g * 7919) % 10000, (ARRAY['EUR','EUR','EUR','GBP','USD','SEK'])[1 + (g * 31) % 6], CASE WHEN g % 50 = 0 THEN 'refunded' WHEN g % 20 = 0 THEN 'failed' ELSE 'settled' END, (g * 104729) % 100000, TIMESTAMP '2026-10-01' + g * interval '2 seconds' FROM generate_series(1, 1000000::bigint) g; VACUUM ANALYZE payments; SELECT pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size('payments')) AS heap, relpages FROM pg_class WHERE relname = 'payments'; SELECT avg(pg_column_size(p.*))::int AS row_bytes, avg(pg_column_size(p.amount_cents))::int AS amount_bytes FROM payments p; SET max_parallel_workers_per_gather = 0; EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS, COSTS OFF, TIMING OFF, SUMMARY OFF) SELECT sum(amount_cents) FROM payments;

sections.h: Neighbouring values look alike, so a column compresses
sections.html:
Put a column's values next to each other and they turn out to be very repetitive. The currency column of a million payments holds four different strings. status holds three. amount_cents holds numbers below 100,000 in 8-byte slots that could hold numbers up to 9 quintillion. created_at rises by 2 seconds per row.

Version 1 runs a general-purpose compressor such as zstd or gzip over each column. The ratio is good, but every scan pays to decompress everything it touches, and reading one value means decompressing the block around it. DuckDB's engineers explained in 2022 why they rely on lighter methods for their tables: general-purpose compressors are expensive to decompress, need blocks of around 256 KB to compress well, and hide the data's structure from the query engine.

Version 2 uses lightweight encodings. Each one is built for one pattern and is cheap enough to decode inside a scan:

  • Dictionary encoding stores each distinct value once, in a sorted list, and replaces every value by its position in the list, a small integer code. Four currencies become codes 0 to 3. Because the list is sorted, currency < 'GBP' can be tested on the codes.
  • Bit-packing stores each number in the fewest bits that hold the largest one. Codes 0 to 3 need 2 bits, so a million currencies take 250 KB. With a frame of reference, the chunk's smallest value is subtracted first: amounts from 0 to 99,999 need 17 bits instead of 64, and the timestamps of one hour need 12 bits once the first second of the hour is subtracted.
  • Run-length encoding (RLE) stores a value once with the number of times it repeats in a row. It wins on sorted or slowly changing columns: a status column sorted by status is three runs, however many rows the table has.

The encodings stack: dictionary codes are then bit-packed or run-length encoded, as the stepper shows. And none of them wins everywhere. A chunk of random 64-bit numbers gains nothing from any of them, and RLE on data without runs makes it bigger. So engines decide per chunk: DuckDB analyses each segment of a column, tries its encodings and keeps the smallest. In the Try it, it chose bit-packing for the four number columns and DICT_FSST for the two text columns: a dictionary whose strings are themselves compressed with FSST, a string compressor that replaces common substrings with one-byte codes. The whole table takes 5.5 MB on disk, against PostgreSQL's 66 MB heap. Your lab's ColumnChunk.of makes the same choice between three encodings.

sections.h: Zone maps let a scan skip chunks
sections.html:
Compression makes each chunk smaller, but WHERE created_at on one day of October still decodes every chunk of created_at to find the rows. The fix costs almost nothing. When the engine writes a chunk, it also notes the chunk's smallest and largest value. That pair is a zone map, also called a min-max index. Before decoding a chunk, the scan compares the chunk's [min, max] with the condition. If the day lies outside it, no row in the chunk can match and the chunk is skipped unread. If the whole chunk lies inside the condition, every row matches, and count(*) can add the chunk's row count without decoding it either.

In the DuckDB demo each row group of 122,880 payments covers about 2.8 days, and a one-day query scans 2 of the 9 row groups, the two that overlap October 15. The other 7 are ruled out by their min and max alone. DuckDB keeps a zone map for every column of every row group without being asked.

Zone maps only work when a column's values follow the order of the rows on disk. Payments arrive in time order, so created_at and id rise from chunk to chunk and each chunk covers a narrow slice. amount_cents is in random order: every chunk holds amounts from almost 0 to almost 100,000, so every zone map overlaps every range and nothing is skipped. The demo shuffles the same rows into a second table, and the one-day query then scans 9 row groups of 9. If you want zone maps to help a column, load the data sorted by it.

PostgreSQL has zone maps as an index type. A BRIN (block range index) stores the min and max of a column for every 128 pages by default. On the 1,000,000 time-ordered payments it takes 24 kB, where a B+tree index on the same column takes 21 MB. The one-day query through it reads 512 of 8,404 heap pages and rechecks the rows in them. On the shuffled copy the same kind of index reads all 8,384 pages. BRIN is a good fit for append-only tables queried by time, such as an audit log or the journal entries of a ledger. A B+tree finds rows more precisely and works in any order, at about 900 times the size.

For October 15 it marked 4 ranges of 128 pages, 512 pages, as possible matches ("lossy" means whole pages, not rows), and the recheck threw away the rows of the neighbouring days. On the shuffled table every range spans the whole month, so the same query read all 8,384 pages and rechecked 1,000,000 rows to keep 43,200. enable_seqscan = off only makes the planner use the index there so you can see this; it would rightly choose a sequential scan.

sections.h: Cloud warehouses keep a zone map for every file they write
sections.html:
Snowflake, Redshift and BigQuery are column stores whose data lives in object storage or managed disks, and the last two sections decide most of what a query costs there. Snowflake cuts every table into micro-partitions of 50 to 500 MB of uncompressed data, stored compressed, each column separately. For every micro-partition it keeps metadata outside the data: each column's range of values and its number of distinct values. A query's WHERE clause is checked against that metadata first, and a micro-partition that can't match is never fetched. Snowflake's own example of the ideal: a year of hourly data, queried for one hour, reads 1/8,760 of the micro-partitions.

Ideal is the catch, and it is the shuffled table from the last section again. Snowflake partitions a table in the order its rows are inserted or loaded. Payments loaded in time order prune well by date. A filter on merchant mostly doesn't, because every micro-partition holds hundreds of merchants and its range for merchant_id covers nearly all of them. Snowflake measures this as clustering depth: for a column, the average number of micro-partitions whose ranges overlap, 1 or more for a populated table, lower is better. Declare a clustering key and Snowflake re-sorts data in the background to keep the depth down, and bills you for the compute. Updates and deletes spread new rows around, so the depth drifts back up over time.

Amazon Redshift does the same with smaller pieces and more control. It stores each column in 1 MB blocks and keeps every block's min and max as metadata, its zone maps. You choose a sort key when you create a table (or let SORTKEY AUTO choose), rows are stored in that order, and a range filter on the sort key skips blocks: AWS's example is five years of data sorted by date, where a one-month query skips up to 98% of the blocks. A compound sort key works like lesson 7's multicolumn index, helping filters on a prefix of its columns. An interleaved sort key weights each column equally, and costs more to keep sorted.

Writes follow the rule from the last section. Changing one value inside a sorted, compressed file means writing a new file, so warehouses buffer new rows and write them out in bulk as new files, the LSM pattern of lesson 5 again. Some changes need no rewrite at all: in Snowflake, deleting every row of a table only changes metadata.

The open version of this design is Parquet files in object storage: row groups with min and max statistics for every column chunk, read by DuckDB, Spark or Trino. The Batch track opens those files and the table formats built on them.

try.title: Predict what a warehouse prunes
steps: No Docker here: work it out on paper, then check the answer. A Snowflake table holds two years of card payments in 2,000 micro-partitions, loaded in time order, so each micro-partition covers about 9 hours.

For each query, estimate how many micro-partitions are read: (a) WHERE created_at on one day; (b) WHERE merchant_id = 'M-0042', a merchant that takes payments every day; (c) WHERE currency = 'SEK', 5% of payments, spread evenly; (d) the same as (b) after adding the clustering key (merchant_id, created_at) and letting Snowflake re-sort, for a table of 10,000 merchants.
Then say which of the four you would expect to get slower over a year of updates to old payments, and why.
try.expect: (a) About 3 or 4: two years is about 17,500 hours in 2,000 micro-partitions, so each covers about 9 hours, and one day overlaps 3 or 4 of them. The zone maps on created_at are narrow because the load order is time order. (b) Almost all 2,000: the merchant appears every day, so its id falls inside nearly every micro-partition's range for merchant_id. Zone maps can only rule out a micro-partition whose range misses the value. (c) Almost all 2,000: SEK is in every micro-partition, and a dictionary or distinct count doesn't change that. A column store still wins here by reading one or two columns of each, not all of them. (d) A handful: sorted by merchant first, each micro-partition holds a few of the 10,000 merchants (about 5 each), so M-0042's rows sit in one or two of them, and their merchant_id ranges rule out the rest. The clustered table is the one that degrades: updates rewrite rows into new micro-partitions in arrival order, ranges start to overlap again, the clustering depth rises, and background reclustering, billed as compute, works to bring it back down. (a) stays good as long as loads stay in time order.

sections.h: Column stores win scans and lose single-row work
sections.html:
Put the pieces together and an analytics scan in a column store touches only the columns the query names, reads them compressed, skips chunks by their zone maps, and hands the rest to a vectorized executor from lesson 9 in batches of a couple of thousand values from one column. DuckDB's vectors hold 2,048 values. Some engines go further and filter the compressed data directly: a condition on currency becomes a comparison of 2-bit codes, and only the row positions that pass are used to fetch values from the other columns. That is called late materialization.

The same design makes single-row work expensive. Changing one payment's status means finding the value inside a compressed chunk, and rewriting a whole chunk for one value is wasteful, so column stores usually record changes on the side, for example a list of deleted row positions, and rewrite chunks later. Rows inserted one at a time form small chunks that compress badly until they are merged. And reading one whole payment reads one chunk from each of six columns, against one page in a heap.

So the two layouts end up in different places in a payments company. The ledger, the idempotency keys and the authorizations stay in a row store such as PostgreSQL or Oracle, where each request touches a few rows by key. Reconciliation, reporting and fraud analysis run on a column store: DuckDB inside a service or a notebook, a warehouse such as Snowflake, Redshift or BigQuery, or Parquet files in object storage read by Spark or Trino. Data moves from one side to the other in batches, through change data capture or a nightly export. PostgreSQL itself stays a row store. Extensions add columnar tables to it, but the heap from lesson 2 is what you get by default.

analogy: A row store is a box of filled-in payment forms, one form per payment. A column store cuts every form into strips, one strip per field, and keeps one binder per field, the strips in the same order. To total the amounts you open one binder instead of reading every form; to read one whole payment you open six binders and find the same position in each. Neat binders also make zone maps easy: write the first and last date on the spine of each date binder and you know which ones to skip. The analogy breaks at compression. A binder of paper strips that all say EUR is as thick as one with mixed currencies, while a column chunk of a thousand EURs becomes one dictionary entry and a run.
world: The payments ledger in PostgreSQL or Oracle is a row store for good reasons: each authorization touches a few rows by key. The trouble starts when the monthly reconciliation runs on the same primary and scans 50 million rows for three columns, competing with live traffic for the buffer pool. Export those rows in batches (a nightly job, or change data capture from the WAL into Kafka) and query them in a column store. For one service, DuckDB embedded in a Quarkus job can query Parquet files in object storage directly, with no database server to run. Sort the files by settlement date or merchant before writing them, and zone maps will skip most of a file for one day or one merchant. Oracle's Database In-Memory option is the same idea inside the row store: it keeps a columnar copy of chosen tables in memory next to the normal row format. In PostgreSQL, a BRIN index on created_at of an append-only audit or event table costs kilobytes and answers time-range queries without a B+tree.
mistake: The common mistake is writing to a column store the way a service writes to PostgreSQL: one INSERT per event, straight from a Kafka consumer, or an UPDATE per status change. Many column stores write each small insert as its own small part or file, which compresses badly and carries its own zone map; updates pile up on the side, and the store spends its time merging what a batch load would have written once. People do it because the client library makes a single-row insert look the same as a batch. The fix is to batch: buffer events and load them thousands at a time (DuckDB's appender or COPY, Parquet files with large row groups), and model status changes as new rows rather than updates. Sort each batch by the column you filter on most, so the zone maps can skip.

compare.note: Both hold the same rows; the difference is which bytes sit next to each other. The row layout makes one row cheap to write and to read whole. The column layout makes one column cheap to scan, and since equal or similar values now sit together, it compresses well. Each layout is slow at the other's job.

worked.title: Bit-pack eight currency codes by hand

steps.say: Eight payments' currencies. Build the sorted dictionary and replace each value by its code.
steps.code:
values:     EUR EUR GBP EUR USD EUR SEK EUR
dictionary: 0 = EUR, 1 = GBP, 2 = SEK, 3 = USD
codes:      0   0   1   0   3   0   2   0

steps.say: The largest code is 3, so each code needs bitsFor(3) = 2 bits. Value i goes to bits 2i and 2i + 1 of one 64-bit word.
OR each code into place with a shift. Only three codes are not zero.
steps.code:
word = (1 shl 4) or (3 shl 8) or (2 shl 12)
     = 16 + 768 + 8192 = 8976
     = 0b10_00_11_00_01_00_00   (pairs from value 6 down to value 0)

steps.say: Read value 4 back: shift it down and keep 2 bits. Then look the code up in the dictionary.

With wider values a code can straddle two words. The lab's decode takes the low part from one word and the high part from the next. For 17-bit amounts, value 3 starts at bit 51 and its top 4 bits are in word 1.
steps.code: val pos = i.toLong() * bits // 3 * 17 = 51 val word = (pos / 64).toInt() // 0 val offset = (pos % 64).toInt() // 51 var x = words[word] ushr offset // 13 low bits if (offset + bits > 64) x = x or (words[word + 1] shl (64 - offset)) // 4 high bits val value = base + (x and ((1L shl bits) - 1))

steps.say: Count the bytes. Plain, the eight strings take 8 x (4 + 3) = 56 bytes. Encoded: the dictionary (4 x 7 = 28 bytes) plus 16 bits of codes. The dictionary is paid once per chunk, so on a chunk of 2,048 values the codes cost 512 bytes against 14,336.
steps.code:
plain:   8 x 7            = 56 bytes
encoded: 28 + 2           = 30 bytes
2,048 values: 28 + 512    = 540 bytes, against 14,336

lab.title: Build a compressed column chunk with zone maps
steps: Read the top of Encodings.kt: the Encoded interface, Plain, bitsFor() and the size formula of each encoding. Run the tests once: all 11 fail.
Write RunLength.encode() and RunLength.decode(). The two run-length tests pass, including a 13,000x smaller sorted status column.
Write BitPacked.encode() and BitPacked.decode(), frame of reference included. The round-trip test tries every width from 1 to 64 bits, so values that straddle two words are covered.
Write Dictionary.encode(), then ColumnChunk.of() in Column.kt, which keeps the smallest of the three encodings and records min and max.
Write Column.countBetween(): skip, count whole, or decode each chunk by its zone map. Run the tests until all 11 pass.
hints: In BitPacked.encode, compute positions with Longs: val pos = i.toLong() * bits. The word is pos / 64 and the offset pos % 64. The spill goes to the next word only when offset + bits > 64, and it is x ushr (64 - offset).
values.max() - base is right even when the range needs all 64 bits: the subtraction wraps, and bitsFor reads the result as unsigned. Decoding adds base back with the same wrap.
For the mask in decode, (1L shl bits) - 1 fails at 64 bits, because a shift by 64 is a shift by 0 on the JVM. Use -1L when bits == 64.
In countBetween, test the skip case first (max < lo || min > hi), then the whole-chunk case (lo <= min && max <= hi), and increment chunksDecoded only when you call decode().

drill.title: Write run-length encoding from memory
drill.prompt: Close the lab. Write encode(input: LongArray): RunLength and RunLength.decode(), where a RunLength holds values: LongArray and lengths: IntArray, one entry per run. Then say how many bytes the lab's format uses for a sorted column of 1,000,000 values with 5 distinct statuses.

answer.html: fun encode(input: LongArray): RunLength { val values = ArrayList<Long>() val lengths = ArrayList<Int>() for (v in input) { if (values.isNotEmpty() && values.last() == v) lengths[lengths.size - 1]++ // same as the left neighbour else { values += v; lengths += 1 } // a new run } return RunLength(values.toLongArray(), lengths.toIntArray()) } fun RunLength.decode(): LongArray { val out = LongArray(lengths.sum()) var pos = 0 for (r in values.indices) { out.fill(values[r], pos, pos + lengths[r]) pos += lengths[r] } return out } // sorted, 5 statuses: 5 runs x (8 + 4) = 60 bytes, against 8,000,000 plain.

recap: A row store keeps whole rows together, so a scan of one column reads every page: 66 MB for a sum over 8 MB of amounts in the Try it. A column store keeps each column's values together and rebuilds rows by position.
Column stores cut tables into row groups (DuckDB: 122,880 rows; Parquet: row groups of column chunks) and encode each column chunk separately.

Dictionary encoding replaces values by codes into a sorted list; bit-packing stores numbers in the fewest bits, after subtracting the chunk's minimum (frame of reference); run-length encoding stores runs of equal values once.
Engines try several encodings per chunk and keep the smallest. DuckDB stored the 1,000,000 payments in 5.5 MB against PostgreSQL's 66 MB heap.

A zone map is a chunk's min and max. A scan skips chunks whose range misses the condition and counts chunks that lie inside it, but only if the column follows the order of the rows on disk. PostgreSQL's BRIN index is a zone map per 128 pages.

Cloud warehouses prune the same way at larger scale: Snowflake keeps value ranges per 50 to 500 MB micro-partition and Redshift min and max per 1 MB block, so clustering and sort keys decide how much a query reads. Column stores stay slow at single-row work, so payments data is copied to them in batches.

explain.prompt: Your team exports 50 million payments a month to Parquet for reconciliation. Explain why a query for one day's EUR settlements reads so little of the file, and what you would change if it read everything.
explain.answer: Parquet stores the rows in row groups, and inside each row group every column is a separate chunk. The query reads only the columns it names, so the other columns cost nothing. Each chunk is encoded: currency as a small dictionary with codes of a few bits, amounts bit-packed after subtracting the chunk's minimum, timestamps the same way, so the bytes read are a fraction of the raw size. Each column chunk also records its min and max. If the file was written in time order, most row groups cover other days, their min and max rule out the requested day, and the reader skips them without reading their data. If the query reads everything, the likely cause is that the rows aren't ordered by settlement date, so every row group spans the whole month and no zone map can rule anything out. I'd sort the export by settlement date (and maybe currency) before writing it, and keep the row groups large enough that each chunk compresses well.

deeper.html:
PAX and row groups. Storing each column of a page or row group separately, so one block still holds whole rows but groups their values by column, was proposed as PAX (Partition Attributes Across) by Ailamaki and colleagues in 2001. Row groups in Parquet and DuckDB are the same idea at a larger scale: a row is never spread across files, yet a scan reads only the columns it needs.

More encodings. Delta encoding stores differences between neighbours, which suits timestamps and sorted ids. Floating-point columns need their own methods; DuckDB has used Chimp, Patas and ALP for them. FSST compresses strings by replacing common substrings of up to 8 bytes with one-byte codes, and keeps each string decodable on its own. Parquet's own encodings include dictionary, a run-length and bit-packing hybrid, and delta encodings, with an optional general-purpose compressor such as zstd on top.

Vectorized scans on compressed data. Because bit-packed and dictionary-coded chunks are arrays of small integers, a filter can compare codes with SIMD instructions several values at a time, and produce a selection vector of matching positions, the same structure lesson 9's batch filter builds.

BigQuery. Google's warehouse stores tables in Capacitor, a column format that grew out of the Dremel paper's techniques for nested and repeated fields; you control its pruning with partitioning and clustering columns, the same trade as a Snowflake clustering key.

Newer file formats. Andy Pavlo's review of 2025 lists several new open columnar formats (FastLanes, Vortex, F3 among them) aimed at faster decoding on modern hardware, and notes that most Parquet files in the wild still use only its 2013 features.
